name: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
title: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
answer: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running AI models on hardware the organization controls, from a workstation under a desk to a rack in a private data center, with no dependency on a public API. In legal operations this includes document review, contract analysis, privilege review, e-discovery, and internal knowledge search where client confidences and matter data cannot leave the firm's boundary. Air-gapped means the system is physically or logically separated from the internet, so updates, telemetry, and model downloads must be moved in by controlled means. The scope also includes the supporting stack: model weights, inference server, storage, identity, logging, and the human workflow around them. It is not the same as a private cloud tenant, because the organization owns the physical and network layer.

sections.body: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running AI models on hardware the organization controls, from a workstation under a desk to a rack in a private data center, with no dependency on a public API. In legal operations this includes document review, contract analysis, privilege review, e-discovery, and internal knowledge search where client confidences and matter data cannot leave the firm's boundary. Air-gapped means the system is physically or logically separated from the internet, so updates, telemetry, and model downloads must be moved in by controlled means. The scope also includes the supporting stack: model weights, inference server, storage, identity, logging, and the human workflow around them. It is not the same as a private cloud tenant, because the organization owns the physical and network layer.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Local deployment runs on owned or leased compute: CPU servers, GPU workstations, or appliance boxes sized to the model. Air-gapped sites often use a dedicated rack with no route to the public internet, separate power and cooling, and removable media or a data diode for approved transfers. Storage holds model weights, vector indexes, matter files, and logs, often encrypted at rest. Identity and access management, backup, and monitoring are part of the infrastructure, because a disconnected system still needs patching, key management, and recovery plans. The hardware choice depends on model size, latency needs, and the volume of documents to process.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams select a model that can run within the available memory and compute, often an open-weight model, then package it with an inference server and a retrieval layer for firm documents. Because there is no live internet, updates and new models arrive through a controlled import process, with checksums, malware scanning, and version records. Workflows are built around batch or interactive use: a lawyer or paralegal submits a query, the system retrieves relevant passages, the model drafts or classifies, and a human reviews the output. Evaluation is done on local test sets that reflect the firm's matters, and prompts, model versions, and retrieval settings are logged so results can be reproduced. The method is closer to running internal software than to calling a vendor's API.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are confidentiality, privilege, data residency, and model provenance. A local or air-gapped setup can reduce exposure to third-party data use, but it does not remove the need for a lawful basis, client consent where required, and clear retention rules. Provenance matters because the organization must know where model weights came from, what license applies, and whether training data or outputs carry restrictions. The site tracks 149 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which is a reminder that copyright, trade secret, and professional responsibility questions follow the model even when it runs on your own hardware. Audit logs, access controls, and human review are the practical controls that make the deployment defensible.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect smaller, more capable open-weight models, better quantization, and inference software that runs well on modest hardware, which will make local deployment practical for more legal teams. Air-gapped environments will likely get more mature tooling for offline updates, model signing, and reproducible builds, because security teams want supply chain evidence. Regulation will keep expanding, and the site already tracks 222 compliance and regulation pages and 7066 state AI bills, so local deployment will be judged against a patchwork of state, federal, and professional rules. The direction is toward hybrid patterns, where sensitive work stays local and less sensitive tasks may use controlled external services, with clear boundaries and logs. The field will remain an infrastructure and governance discipline as much as a modeling one.
